concept.name: Smart contract
concept.definition: A smart contract is a program deployed to a blockchain — a collection of code (functions) and data (state) at a specific address — that executes automatically and exactly as written when called by a transaction.
concept.intuition: A vending machine for logic: given the right inputs and fee, a guaranteed, unstoppable output, with no operator able to intervene.
concept.mechanics: Developers compile code (e.g. Solidity) to EVM bytecode and deploy it via a transaction; the contract then exists as an account type with a balance and storage but no private key. Users and other contracts invoke its functions by sending transactions that pay gas; execution is deterministic and replicated by every node, and deployed code cannot be altered by default.
concept.failure_modes: Bugs are immutable — exploits like re-entrancy or logic errors can drain contracts with no way to patch or reverse; contracts cannot fetch off-chain data themselves and inherit the risks of whatever oracle they trust.
concept.misconceptions: Smart contracts are neither 'smart' nor legal contracts — they only execute code, cannot interpret intent, and cannot access real-world data without an oracle. 'Code is law' fails badly when the code has bugs.
concept.example: A simple contract might hold 100 cupcake balances and release one to any caller who sends 1 ETH; once deployed, no one — including its creator — can change the 1 ETH price or freeze the cupcakes.
